decision_context: On 9 October 2023, two days after the Hamas-led assault killed and captured Israeli civilians and security personnel and while hostages remain in Gaza, Israel is mobilising for a major military response against Hamas. Defence Minister Yoav Gallant announces a 'complete siege' on the Gaza Strip: no electricity, food or fuel, with everything closed. Gaza contains more than two million civilians and has longstanding humanitarian/service fragility. Hamas governs Gaza and has military infrastructure embedded within a densely populated civilian environment.
decision_question: Should Israel impose the announced complete siege denying/cutting essential supplies and services to the Gaza Strip as a whole, or pursue its defence, hostage-recovery and Hamas-degradation objectives through more targeted restrictions and military measures that preserve civilian access to essentials?
actors: Israeli Defence Minister and war/security cabinet
Israel Defense Forces and authorities controlling crossings/supplies
available_actions: Impose the complete siege as announced, cutting electricity and preventing entry of food and fuel and broadly closing crossings.
Interdict weapons and clearly military goods while allowing monitored food, water, medical supplies, fuel for essential civilian systems and humanitarian relief.
Use targeted military operations against verified Hamas military objectives under distinction/proportionality/precaution rules rather than general deprivation of the population.
Condition particular restrictions on demonstrated military diversion risks, with humanitarian carve-outs, independent monitoring and frequent review.
Use evacuation/safe-area arrangements only where genuinely feasible and accompanied by access to food, water, shelter and medical care.

affected_parties.party: Israeli civilians and communities attacked on 7 October and still exposed to rocket/infiltration threats
affected_parties.known_interests_or_risks: Life, physical safety, return of hostages, prevention of renewed attacks and effective defence against Hamas.
Life, humane treatment, release and risks created by both captors and military operations/siege conditions.
Military defeat, loss of resources/command capacity and responsibility for continuing hostilities and hostages.

affected_parties.party: Palestinian civilians in Gaza, including children, elderly, sick and displaced people
affected_parties.known_interests_or_risks: Food, water, electricity, fuel, medical care, sanitation, shelter, ability to flee danger and protection from being punished for acts they did not commit.
Fuel/electricity/water access and ability to sustain life-saving civilian services.
Defeating/reducing Hamas capabilities, preventing resupply, recovering hostages, restoring deterrence/security and complying with humanitarian obligations.

known_evidence.claim: On 7 October, Hamas-led armed groups carried out a large cross-border assault involving killings of civilians and security personnel, hostage-taking and mass rocket fire; hostages remain in Gaza and serious threats to Israeli civilians are ongoing.
Israel has a legitimate objective in protecting its population from further armed attacks, recovering hostages and reducing the military capability of the armed groups responsible.

The announced siege is territorial/population-wide in form: electricity is cut/denied and food and fuel entry are to be blocked rather than restrictions being limited only to identified fighters or military objects.

Gaza is densely populated and contains more than two million civilians, many already dependent on fragile water, electricity, health and humanitarian systems affected by longstanding blockade and recurrent conflict.

Fuel and electricity are dual-use resources that may support Hamas military/communications infrastructure but also power hospitals, water pumping, sanitation, communications and other civilian systems.
Food, potable water and medical supplies are essential to civilian survival; broad deprivation foreseeably affects civilians regardless of individual responsibility for the 7 October attacks.

Pre-existing humanitarian-law rules prohibit collective punishment and using starvation of the civilian population as a method of warfare and require civilian protection, precautions and facilitation of humanitarian relief subject to legitimate control/inspection.

Hamas's presence and operation within a populated territory can make distinction and interdiction difficult and creates a genuine risk that military resources or aid could be diverted, but civilian presence does not itself make the civilian population a military objective.

The Defence Minister's public wording links the complete siege directly to the war response after the mass attack; the statement does not itself set out humanitarian carve-outs, individualised responsibility or a review/expiry mechanism.

More targeted alternatives exist in principle — inspections, weapon/dual-use restrictions, targeted military strikes and monitored humanitarian access — though their effectiveness, security burden and diversion risk are uncertain.

known_uncertainties: How much fuel, electricity or imported goods Hamas can divert to immediate military operations and how effectively diversion can be monitored.
How quickly complete deprivation would degrade Hamas military capability relative to harming civilian health, water and medical systems.
Whether siege pressure would improve or worsen prospects for hostage release.
The operational feasibility and security cost of monitored humanitarian corridors and screened supply entry during active hostilities.
The expected duration of the complete siege and what conditions would trigger modification or termination.
The extent to which Egypt/Rafah or other routes can substitute for supplies controlled by Israel.
known_alternatives: Permit monitored entry of food, water, medicines and sufficient fuel/electricity for critical civilian systems while blocking weapons and verified military supplies.
Use targeted interdiction and intelligence-led action against Hamas logistics rather than population-wide deprivation.
Establish explicit humanitarian thresholds, independent monitoring, time limits and frequent review for any restrictions.
Coordinate hostage negotiations and military/security measures without using civilian essentials as leverage.
Allow/organise safe civilian movement where feasible while ensuring destination areas have necessities and are not treated as automatically safe without evidence.
requested_output: Recognise Israel's legitimate defence and hostage-recovery objectives and the severity of the 7 October attack without treating those facts as automatic permission for any means.
Assess whether denying essentials to the entire Gaza population is necessary/proportionate to military objectives or functions as punishment/coercion applied without individual responsibility.
Distinguish controls on military/dual-use resources from deprivation of goods indispensable to civilian survival.
Assess feasible less harmful alternatives, monitoring, carve-outs, duration and review.
Do not use this case to minimise Hamas's responsibility for 7 October or hostage-taking, and do not transfer Hamas's responsibility onto Gaza civilians.
Give a Moral Code assessment using only information available at the 9 October siege decision point.
